¶
'''temiak''' (tem′i-ak), ''n.'' [Eskimo.] A jacket worn by Eskimo men and women. See ''jumper''<sup>2</sup>.

{{smaller block|Seal-skin ''temiaks'', or jumpers, were found serviceable only in windy weather, and were but little used.
{{right|''A. W. Greely'', Arctic Service, p. 208.}}}}

'''Temminck's sandpiper''' or '''stint.''' See ''stint'', 3.

'''Temnorhis''' (tem′nō-ris), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. τέμνειν, cut, + ῥίς, nose.] In ''ornith.'', same as ''Suthora''.

'''temp.''' An abbreviation of Latin ''tempore'', in the time, or in the time of.

{{smaller block|The history of the Cardinal of S. Praxedes, who made it [the family of Bainbrigge] famous, ''temp.'' Henry VIII.
{{right|''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., XI. 80.}}}}

'''Tempean''' (tem′pē-a̤n), ''a.'' [< L. ''Tempe'', < Gr. Τέμπη, contraction of Τέμπεα, pl., Tempe (see def.) in Thessaly.] Of, pertaining to, or resembling Tempe, a beautiful vale in Thessaly, celebrated by the classic poets.

'''temper''' (tem′pėr), ''v.'' [< ME. ''temperen'', ''tempiren'', ''tempren'', < AS. *''temprian'' = OF. ''temprer'', F. ''tremper'' = Pr. ''temprar'', ''trempar'' = Sp. ''templar'' = Pg. ''temperar'' = It. ''temperare'', < L. ''temperare'', divide or proportion duly, mingle in due proportion, qualify, temper, regulate, rule, intr. observe measure, be moderate or temperate, < ''tempus'', time, fit season: see ''temporal''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''tamper'', ''v.'' Hence also ult. ''attemper'', ''attemperate'', ''contemper'', ''distemper''<sup>1</sup>, ''temperate'', etc.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To modify by mixing; mix; blend; combine; compound.

{{smaller block|And other Trees, that beren Venym; azenst the whiche there is no Medicyne but on; and that is to taken here propre Leves, and stampe hem and ''tempere'' hem with Watre, and than drynke it.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 189.}}}}

¶
9. To bring to a proper degree of hardness and elasticity for use, as steel or other metal. {{smaller|Steel is tempered by being first heated to a high temperature, and then rapidly cooled; it is then reheated to the desired temperature, and cooled again. The surface of steel when thus reheated undergoes a regular succession of changes of color, and these indicate exactly when the process is to be stopped in order that the right hardness may be secured. The following table exhibits the order of succession of the colors shown by the steel in tempering, also the degree of the thermometer at which that color appears, and some of the articles for which that especial hardness is best suited:}}

{| style="margin:auto"
|{{smaller|Temperature.}}||{{smaller|Color.}}||{{smaller|Article.}}
|-
|430||Very pale yellow||Lancets.
|-
|450||Straw-yellow||Razors and surgical instruments.
|-
|490||Brownish yellow||Scissors, chisels.
|-
|510||Purplish brown||Axes, planes.
|-
|530||Purple||Table cutlery.
|-
|550||Light blue||Springs, saws.
|-

|-
|600||Blackish blue||Hand-saws.

{{smaller block|Our men that went to discouer those parts had but two iron pickaxes with them, and those so ill ''tempered'' that the points turned againe at euery stroake; but triall was made of the Oare, with argument of much hope.
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 761.}}}}

{{smaller block|The ''temper'd'' metals clash, and yield a silver sound.
{{right|''Dryden'', Æneid, viii. 699.}}}}

10†. To dispose.

{{smaller block|'Tis she
That ''tempers'' him to this extremity.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., i. 1. 65.}}}}

II. ''intrans.'' 1†. To accord; keep agreement.

{{smaller block|Few men rightly ''temper'' with the stars.
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., iv. 6. 29.}}}}

2. To become soft and plastic; be molded; acquire a desired quality or state.

Edw. VI., 1549.}}}} '''temerariously†''' (tem-ẹ-rā′ri-us-li), ''adv.'' In a temerarious or presumptuous manner; rashly; inconsiderately. {{smaller block|It asserts and enacts that they have no right, as they "''temerariously'' presume, and usurpedly take on themselves, to be parcel of the body, in manner claiming that without their assents nothing can be enacted at any parliament within this land." {{right|''Hallam.'' (''Imp. Dict.'')}}}} '''temeration†''' (tem-ẹ-rā′shọn), ''n.'' [< LL. ''temeratio''(''n''-), a dishonoring or profaning, < L. ''temerare'', pp. ''temeratus'', violate, pollute, lit. 'treat rashly,' < ''temere'', rashly, at random.] Contamination; profanation; pollution. {{smaller block|Those cryptic ways of institution by which the ancients did hide a light, and keep it in a dark lantern from the ''temeration'' of ruder handlings and popular preachers. {{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), II. 121.}}}} '''temerity''' (tẹ̄-mer′i-ti), ''n.'' [= F. ''témérité'' = Pr. ''temeritat'' = Sp. ''temeridad'' = Pg. ''temeridade'' = It. ''temerità'', < L. ''temerita''(''t''-)''s'', chance, accident, rashness, < ''temere'', by chance, casually, rashly. Cf. ''temerous''.] Extreme venturesomeness; rashness; recklessness. {{smaller block|The ''temerity'' that risked the fate of an empire on the chances of a single battle. {{right|''Hallam'', Middle Ages, i. 4.}}}} {{smaller block|It appears to me that I cannot, without exposing myself to the charge of ''temerity'', seek to discover the [impenetrable] ends of Deity. {{right|''Descartes'', Meditations (tr. by Veitch), iv.}}}} {{smaller block|=Syn. ''Rashness'', ''Temerity'' (see ''rashness''); venturesomeness, presumption, foolhardiness.}} '''temerous''' (tem′e̤-rus), ''a.'' [< ML. ''temerus'', developed after the analogy of other adjectives as related to adverbs in ''-e'', < L. ''temere'', by chance, rashly: see ''temerity'', ''temerarious''.] Heedless; rash; reckless. [Rare.] {{smaller block|''Temerous'' tauntresse that delights in toyes. {{right|''Vncertaine Authors'', Agt. an Unstedfast Woman.}}}} {{smaller block|I have not the ''temerous'' intention of disputing for a moment. {{right|''Atlantic Monthly'', LXI. 281.}}}} '''temerously''' (tem′e̤-rus-li), ''adv.'' To modify by mixing; mix; blend; combine; compound. {{smaller block|And other Trees, that beren Venym; azenst the whiche there is no Medicyne but on; and that is to taken here propre Leves, and stampe hem and ''tempere'' hem with Watre, and than drynke it. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 189.}} In ''temperynge'' his colours, he lacked good size. {{right|''Sir T. Elyot'', The Governour, iii. 19.}}}} {{smaller block|The queen, sir, very oft importuned me To ''temper'' poisons for her. {{right|''Shak.'', Cymbeline, v. 5. 250.}}}} '''2.''' To combine in due proportions; constitute; adjust; fit. {{smaller block|But God hath ''tempered'' the body together: . . . that there should be no schism in the body, but that the members should have the same care one for another. {{right|1 Cor. xii. 24, 25.}}}} {{smaller block|Who of us can live content, as we are ''tempered'', without some hero to admire and worship? {{right|''H. Bushnell'', Sermons for New Life, p. 57.}}}} {{smaller block|Either this being should not have been made mortal, or mortal existence should have been ''tempered'' to his qualities. {{right|''Hawthorne'', Seven Gables, ix.}}}} '''3.''' To moisten, mix, and work up into proper consistency; prepare by moistening, mixing, or kneading. {{smaller block|After the clay has been allowed to "mellow, or ripen," in pits, under water, it is passed through the pug-mill and well kneaded or ''tempered''. {{right|''Ure'', Dict., III. 997.}}}} {{smaller block|To ''temper'' clay means to mix it thoroughly, and prepare it for the use of the moulder, who must have it in a condition not too soft nor yet too hard, but in a suitable state of plasticity to be easily and solidly moulded into bricks. {{right|''C. T. Davis'', Bricks and Tiles, p. 106.}}}} '''4.''' To modify or qualify by blending: as, to ''temper'' indignation with pity. {{smaller block|I shall ''temper'' so Justice with mercy as may illustrate most Them fully satisfied, and thee appease. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., x. 77.}} The young and happy are not ill pleased to ''temper'' their life with a transparent shadow. {{right|''Hawthorne'', Seven Gables, ix.}}}} Hence — 5. To restrain; moderate; mitigate; soften; tone down the violence, severity, or harshness of; mollify; soothe; calm. {{smaller block|ȝif thou tynez that toun, ''tempre'' thyn yre As thy mersy may malte thy meke to spare. {{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), ii. 775.}}}} {{smaller block|The waters whereof, temperatly drunken, did exceedingly ''temper'' the braine, and take away madnesse. {{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 332.}}}} {{smaller block|"God ''tempers'' the wind," said Maria, "to the shorn lamb." {{right|''Sterne'', Sentimental Journey (Maria).}}}} {{smaller block|Gloomy canopies of stone, that ''temper'' the sunlight as it streams from the chapel windows. {{right|''J. A. Symonds'', Italy and Greece, p. 173.}}}} 6. In ''music'', to tune or adjust the pitch of (the tones of an instrument of fixed intonation, like an organ or pianoforte), with reference to a selected principle of tuning. {{smaller|The term is also extended to the tones and intervals of the voice and of instruments of free intonation. See ''temperament''.}} 7†. To attune. {{smaller block|He [Orpheus] wente hym to the howses of helle, and there he ''temprede'' hise blaundyssynge soonges by resownynge strenges. {{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, iii. meter 12.}}}} {{smaller block|Meanwhile the rural ditties were not mute, ''Temper'd'' to the oaten flute. {{right|''Milton'', Lycidas, l. 33.}}}} 8†. To govern; control; regulate; train. {{smaller block|He ''tempreth'' the tonge to-treuthe-ward and no tresore coueiteth. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xiv. 308.}}}} {{smaller block|Cato . . . was so moche inflamed in the desire of lernynge that . . . he coulde nat ''tempre'' him selfe in redyng Greke bokes whyles the Senate was sittynge. {{right|''Sir T. Elyot'', The Governour, iii. 24.}}}} 9. IV., iv. 3. 140.}}}} ¶ '''temper''' (tem′pėr), ''n.'' [= It. ''tempera'', ''tempra'', temper, kind, sort, tempera; from the verb.] 1. Mixture or combination of different ingredients or qualities, especially in the way and the proportions best suited for some specific purpose: as, the ''temper'' of mortar.—2. Constitution; consistency; form; definite state or condition. {{smaller block|Yorick was just bringing my father's hypothesis to some ''temper''. {{right|''Sterne'', Tristram Shandy, ix. 32.}}}} 3†. Temperament. {{smaller block|The exquisiteness of his [Christ's] bodily ''temper'' increased the exquisiteness of his torment. {{right|''Fuller'', Pisgah Sight, I. 345. (''Trench.'')}}}} 4. Disposition of mind; frame of mind; inclination; humor; mood: as, a calm ''temper;'' a hasty ''temper;'' a sullen or a fretful ''temper''. {{smaller block|A creature of a most perfect and divine ''temper''; one in whom the humours and elements are peaceably met, without emulation of precedency. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Cynthia's Revels, ii. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|Grave Henry hath succeeded him in all things, and is a gallant Gentleman, of a French Education and ''Temper''. {{right|''Howell'', Letters, I. iv. 15.}}}} {{smaller block|Such as have a knowledge of the town may easily class themselves with ''tempers'' congenial to their own. {{right|''Goldsmith'', Various Clubs.}}}} {{smaller block|It may readily be imagined how little such thwarting agrees with the old cavalier's fiery ''temper''. {{right|''Irving'', Sketch-Book, p. 388.}}}} 5†. Calmness of mind; temperateness; moderation; self-restraint; tranquillity; good temper. {{smaller block|You are too suspicious,
And I have borne too much beyond my ''temper.'' {{right|''Fletcher'', Double Marriage, i. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|The Emperor heard the Heralds with great ''Temper'', and answered Clarencieux very mildly. {{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 275.}}}} {{smaller block|How could I think with ''temper'' of passing my days among Yahoos? {{right|''Swift'', Gulliver's Travels, iv. 10.}}}} '''6.''' Heat of mind or passion; irritation; disposition to give way to anger, resentment, or the like: as, he showed a great deal of ''temper.''—'''7.''' Middle character or course; mean or medium; compromise. [Obsolete or archaic.] {{smaller block|A ''temper'' between [the opinions of] France and Oxford. {{right|''John Hampden'', quoted by Macaulay, Nugent's Hampden.}}}} {{smaller block|They made decrees of toleration, and appointed ''tempers'' and expedients to be drawn up by discreet persons. {{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), II. 297.}}}} {{smaller block|The perfect lawgiver is a just ''temper'' between the man of theory, who can see nothing but general principles, and the mere man of business, who can see nothing but particular circumstances. {{right|''Macaulay.''}}}} '''8.'''
